drills.q: Why can a black-box credit model be outright illegal to deploy for adverse decisions, not just 'less transparent'?
drills.a: ECOA/Regulation B (12 CFR 1002.9) requires a creditor to give specific, accurate, principal reasons for an adverse action -- not a generic statement or 'the algorithm decided.' If a model genuinely cannot produce a faithful reason tied to its actual decision process, the creditor cannot satisfy this statutory requirement regardless of accuracy. CFPB Circular 2026-03 (May 2026) explicitly states model complexity/proprietary architecture does not excuse this duty.

drills.q: Compute the four-fifths-rule adverse impact ratio for a model approving 60% of Group A and 40% of Group B, and explain whether proof of intent is required to flag this.
drills.a: Adverse impact ratio = 40%/60% = 0.667 (66.7%), below the 80% threshold, flagging potential disparate impact. No proof of intentional discrimination is required -- disparate-impact liability applies to facially neutral models producing disproportionate outcomes regardless of intent or whether protected features were used directly.

drills.q: A credit model has zero protected-class features yet fails four-fifths-rule testing. Explain why, and how you'd detect this in a large feature set with no single obvious proxy.
drills.a: This is the signature of proxy discrimination: features correlated with protected-class membership (zip code, alternative data, alma mater) can reproduce disparate outcomes without the model ever using the protected attribute directly. Detect it by testing model OUTCOMES (adverse-impact ratios by protected class on actual decisions), not by auditing individual features for correlation, since disparate impact can emerge from the combined effect of many weakly-correlated features.

drills.q: What happened to CFPB AI adverse-action guidance between May 2025 and May 2026, and did the underlying legal requirement change during that gap?
drills.a: Circular 2023-03 was withdrawn May 12, 2025 as part of a mass rollback of 67 guidance documents amid CFPB funding/staffing pressures. Circular 2026-03 (May 5, 2026) reaffirmed the identical substantive position. The underlying statute (ECOA, Regulation B 12 CFR 1002.9) was never repealed and remained in force the entire time -- withdrawing guidance doesn't repeal a statute.

drills.q: Explain why SHAP-based reason codes are a real (not just theoretical) compliance risk for ECOA adverse-action notices, and what the interpretable-by-design alternative is.
drills.a: SHAP is a post-hoc approximation of feature contribution using a chosen background distribution, not the model's actual internal decision logic -- different configuration choices can produce different top reason codes, and explanations can be unstable near decision boundaries. Regulation B requires the actual, specific, principal reasons, so an unfaithful SHAP code is real exposure. Alternative: interpretable-by-design models (scorecards, monotonic-constrained GBMs, GAMs) where feature contributions are exact and stable, not approximated.

drills.q: What is the EU AI Act's classification for credit-scoring systems, and what did the Digital Omnibus change in 2026?
drills.a: Credit-scoring/creditworthiness-evaluation systems are classified high-risk under Annex III, requiring risk management, data governance, technical documentation, and human oversight. The Digital Omnibus (final EU approval June 2026) deferred these obligations from August 2, 2026 to December 2, 2027 -- a 16-month extension, not a removal of the obligation.

drills.q: Work the fraud-detection base-rate example: 1,000,000 transactions, 0.1% fraud prevalence, model recall 80%, false-positive rate 0.5%. Compute precision and explain the practical implication.
drills.a: 1,000 fraud cases (0.1% of 1M), 999,000 legitimate. True positives = 800 (80% recall). False positives = 999,000*0.005 = 4,995. Total flagged = 5,795. Precision = 800/5,795 = 13.8%. Implication: even with a seemingly low 0.5% false-positive rate, over 86% of fraud alerts are actually legitimate transactions -- the base-rate effect explains why investigation teams face alert fatigue despite reasonable-looking model metrics.

drills.q: Why does AML transaction monitoring have a fundamentally different false-positive/negative cost structure than fraud detection, and why do production AML systems still layer ML on top of rules rather than fully replacing them?
drills.a: Fraud false positives cost friction/revenue (tunable business tradeoff). AML false negatives carry direct BSA regulatory/criminal liability, pushing legacy rule-based systems toward >90% false-positive rates since under-alerting is more dangerous. ML is layered on top of rules for triage because regulators expect an auditable rule-based floor -- a purely ML-driven miss is harder to defend to an examiner than a documented rule-based miss.

drills.q: A lender wants to use alternative data (utility/rent payments, cash-flow history) to extend credit to thin-file applicants. What fair-lending risk does this introduce, and does improving aggregate access resolve it?
drills.a: Alternative data sources can correlate with protected-class membership through geography, employment type, or banking-access patterns -- the same proxy-discrimination risk as traditional features. Improving aggregate access does not automatically resolve fair-lending risk: a model can improve access overall while still showing disparate impact on specific decision margins (who's approved vs still denied) or pricing/terms -- requires outcome-level disparate-impact testing across the full decision, not just the headline approval-rate.

drills.q: Design question: your CEO wants to ship a more accurate but genuinely less-explainable deep learning underwriting model over an interpretable alternative. How do you handle it, and how does this shape your architecture choices from the start?
drills.a: Treat the adverse-action-reason-code requirement as a hard architectural constraint decided at model-selection time, not a bolt-on: use an interpretable-by-design model, or if a more complex model is justified by material accuracy gain, build and validate a stability-tested explanation pipeline BEFORE it generates real adverse decisions. Quantify the accuracy gain (reduced default losses) against the specific legal exposure (CFPB Circular 2026-03: complexity doesn't excuse compliance) -- invest in the explanation infrastructure up front rather than shipping first and fixing explainability later, since remediating live legally-deficient adverse-action notices (including liability for past decisions) is far more expensive.
